newsitem.title: DENMARK: Clinton hails "new era of promise".
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails "new era of promise".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton ended a European trip on Saturday by predicting NATO expansion would bring a "new era of promise."
But he acknowledged on the final leg of his tour in Denmark that his deadline for a U.S. withdrawal from a NATO peacekeeping mission in Bosnia might not be met.

Beaming as he was welcomed by an enthusiastic throng waving Danish and American flags, Clinton was introduced by Prime Minister Paul Nyrup Rasmussen as the "president of peace" for his role in setting U.S. policy since the end of the Cold War.

"We gather today at the end of what will long be remembered as a week in which a new era of promise was launched for all Europe," Clinton said, referring to the decision by NATO leaders earlier in the week in Madrid to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance.
"This week in Madrid, we adopted NATO to meet the new security challenges of the 21st Century," he said.
The security obligations of the United States, however, cast some stark light on Clinton's upbeat view of the future.

Asked during a photo opportunity with Rasmussen about withdrawal of American peacekeeping forces from the NATO peacekeeping mission in Bosnia, Clinton indicated that his target of June, 1998 might not be met.
"I believe the present operation will have run its course by then and then we will have to discuss what, if any, involvement the U.S. should have," he told reporters.

The U.S. House of Representatives last month voted to cut off funding for U.S. troops serving in a Bosnia stabilisation force (SFOR) next June and the Senate on Friday strongly urged, but did not require, a pullout by then.

"I will say this, our work there with the SFOR...we have fewer troops there now than when we started, it's been much less expensive and much less hazardous to America than a resumption of full-scale war would be," Clinton said.
"I think its been a very good thing we've done and I hope the American people would be very proud of it," he added.

The exchange stamped an air of harsh reality on a trip that had taken on a special glow for Clinton. He overcame a bid at the NATO summit to add Romania and Slovenia to the list of countries being invited to join the alliance.
After the summit he went to Poland, Romania and then Denmark -- each time giving public addresses that generated increasingly enthusiastic crowds at each stop.

The issue of Bosnia stands as a potential obstacle to Clinton in his drive to win U.S. Senate support for expansion of NATO -- a debate that may well begin about the same time as the June, 1998 target for ending American participation in the Bosnia mission.
Opponents of expanding NATO argue in part that the United States should be careful about increasing its military obligations in Europe.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry was asked repeatedly if Clinton was likely to keep U.S. forces in Bosnia beyond next June, but declined to address the questions specifically.
"There has been nothing advanced in formal planning," he told reporters during a briefing in Copenhagen.

Clinton on Friday said the drive by NATO to arrest accused Bosnia war criminals, which included an operation against two Serb suspects by British soldiers two days ago, was part of an overall attempt to salvage the Dayton peace accords.
"We basically believe that we have to make an effort to save the Dayton process," Clinton told reporters on Air Force One on his way to Denmark from Romania.
Clinton on Saturday left Denmark to return to Washington.
